sections.heading: Why Some Files Must Be Locked
paragraphs: Not every PDF is meant for open eyes. Bank statements, signed contracts, medical results and unreleased reports travel better sealed. [protect-pdf:Password-protecting a PDF] wraps the content so only people with the key can open it.
Encryption is also about confidence in transit — email is leakier than we assume, and a locked file survives a wrong Cc gracefully.
ChooseTools encrypts PDFs locally in your browser. Set a password, download the protected file, and no version of your document has ever left your device.

sections.heading: How to Add a Password to a PDF
paragraphs: Locking your file takes less than a minute.
Upload your PDF and choose a strong password — we advise a genuinely random phrase. Confirm it, and the tool encrypts the document in the browser and delivers a protected PDF for download.
Because encryption runs locally, the password and the file both exist only on your machine. Share the password with recipients through a separate channel.

sections.heading: Strong Passwords for Real Protection
paragraphs: Encryption strength depends on password quality: short, dictionary words undo even good encryption algorithms.
Use a long passphrase unique to the document — twelve or more characters mixing cases and numbers — and store it in your password manager.
If you need a strong starting point, the suite's [password-generator:password generator] creates random, memorable passphrases in a second.

sections.heading: What PDF Encryption Actually Does
paragraphs: PDF encryption scrambles the document content so that opening the file without the correct password yields only gibberish. Strong algorithms such as AES-256 with a sufficiently long password resist brute-force attacks for practical purposes.

The security level matters: older 40-bit and 128-bit encryption standards are now considered weak, while modern 256-bit AES encryption is the current best practice. The output uses strong encryption so the protected file meets today's security expectations.
Encryption does not print a watermark onto your document or alter its layout; it simply gates access. Recipients who enter the correct password open and use the PDF exactly as you created it.

sections.heading: Sensitive Documents Across Every Scenario
paragraphs: Human-resources shares offer letters, an accountant distributes yearly summaries, lawyers exchange draft agreements — all demand a password.
Encryption layers cleanly with other protections: redact with [pdf-redaction:PDF redaction] the most sensitive content, flatten with [flatten-pdf:flatten PDF], and then lock the final file.
The locked PDF opens only with the password and remains unreadable to anyone else, email filters included.

sections.heading: Sharing the Password Safely
paragraphs: Sending the password in the same email as the PDF defeats the entire purpose of encryption, because a mailbox compromise reveals both at once. Send the document to one channel and the password through a completely separate one, such as an SMS text or a phone call.

Mobile messaging apps with end-to-end encryption offer a more secure option for the passphrase delivery. Password managers can also share the credential directly with a recipient rather than transmitting the plain-text secret.

If you must store the password, keep it in a password manager rather than as a note attached to the file. This keeps the secret organized and retrievable if you send the same document to more than one person.

sections.heading: Local Encryption Respects Your Data
paragraphs: Sending a confidential PDF to a cloud service to have it "protected" undermines the point entirely. Here, encryption happens on your machine.
No watermark, no account, no reuse of your content, and identical behavior on Windows, macOS, Linux and mobile browsers.
Free and private, protecting documents is available the moment you need it, from any device.

sections.heading: Protection as the Last Gate
paragraphs: Most workflows treat encryption as the exit polish: finalize with [pdf-editor:editing], [compress-pdf:compress] for size, then lock before dispatch.
Keep the password and the recipient list organized, and the same protected file can circulate without ever losing its confidentiality.
The takeaway: with free browser-based encryption, every sensitive PDF leaves your desk sealed.

faqs.q: Does password protection actually encrypt the PDF content?
faqs.a: Yes. The tool applies real PDF encryption keyed by your password; the document cannot be opened without the correct passphrase.

faqs.q: What are the best practices for the password I set?
faqs.a: Use a long, unique passphrase of at least twelve characters mixing letters, numbers and symbols, stored in a password manager and shared with recipients via a secure channel.

faqs.q: Is PDF encryption available for free and in private?
faqs.a: Yes. Everything runs locally in your browser with no uploads, watermarks or accounts — only you ever handle the document.

faqs.q: Can I remove the password later?
faqs.a: Yes. Open the document with the password you set and use a decryption or unlock feature to produce a new unprotected PDF when the file no longer needs protection.

faqs.q: Will the encrypted PDF look different from the original?
faqs.a: No. Encryption changes how the file is opened, not how it looks. The document content, layout and formatting are preserved exactly.
